turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am not so entirely without feelings as you suppose; but it has been my misfortune to be surrounded by people who are not in the habit of making allowances for my feelings.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You expect me to forgive and forget your past behavior simply because you now claim to have feelings for me?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be swayed by your words, Mr. Darcy. Your past behavior towards me and my family has been nothing short of insulting, and I will not be persuaded to forget it merely because you now claim to have feelings for me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You would have me believe that your feelings for me have suddenly changed simply because you now find me tolerable as a wife? I think not, Mr. Darcy.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not a prize to be won, Mr. Darcy, and I will not be caught up in your schemes simply because you have changed your mind about me. Your words are empty and insincere, and I will not be swayed by them.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I find it quite astonishing that you would so readily dismiss my declarations of affection, when they come from one such as myself, a gentleman of considerable standing and reputation.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have no interest in your gentlemanly standing or reputation, Mr. Darcy, and I will not be swayed by them. My regard for you is precisely zero, and I will not be caught up in your schemes to win me over. You may have money and title, but you have none of the qualities I value in a partner, and I will not settle for less.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not deceived by your attempts to manipulate me with your wealth and influence, Mr. Darcy. I see through your schemes and I will not be swayed by them.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be lectured to by you, Mr. Darcy, about what I should or should not find acceptable in a partner. My judgment is not so easily swayed by your condescending words.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I find it quite vexing to be so summarily rejected, especially after I have professed my deepest feelings to you. Your lack of gratitude and discernment is truly surprising, given the extent to which I have gone to demonstrate my suitability as a suitor.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your sentiments, Miss Elizabeth, are as unpredictable as they are unbecoming. I must confess that I am beginning to doubt whether it is wise for me to continue pursuing a union with one who so manifestly lacks a sense of propriety and decorum.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist, Miss Elizabeth, that you reconsider your decision. Your rejection of me is not only unwarranted, but also a slight to my honor and character.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I find your continued refusal to consider my proposal to be a reflection of your own limited understanding of the world and your place within it.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your honor and character? Really, Mr. Darcy? You think a proposal and a few empty words constitute a respectable attempt to win my hand?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I fail to see how you can so cavalierly dismiss my declarations of affection, Miss Elizabeth, when I have gone to such great lengths to secure your family's financial well-being and social standing.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have no desire to be bound to a man who has consistently shown me disdain and disrespect, Mr. Darcy. Your attempts to secure my family's financial well-being are hardly a gesture of affection, but rather a means to further your own social standing and family interests.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished that you would so callously equate my efforts to improve your family's circumstances with mere self-interest, Miss Elizabeth. It is a gross misinterpretation, and one that speaks poorly of your capacity for understanding.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I fail to see how you can be so oblivious to the harm you've caused my family and me, Mr. Darcy. Your 'efforts' to improve our circumstances are nothing but a thinly veiled attempt to erase the memories of your past behavior. I will not be swayed by empty words and half-hearted apologies.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I would rather die than accept a proposal from a man who has treated me with such disdain and disrespect, Mr. Darcy. Your words are as empty as your apology, and I will not be swayed by them.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I had hoped for a more... gracious reception of my proposal. Your continued rejection of me is a source of great distress, and I fear it may prove a lasting blow to my... tender sensibilities.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
